**Space Shuttle _Discovery_** ([Orbiter Vehicle Designation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Vehicle_Designation "Orbiter Vehicle Designation"): **OV-103**) is a retired American [Space Shuttle orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter"). The [spaceplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceplane "Spaceplane") was one of the [orbiters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter") from [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program") and the third of five fully operational orbiters to be built.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-ov103-2) Its first mission, [STS-41-D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D "STS-41-D"), flew from August 30 to September 5, 1984. Over 27 years of service it launched and landed 39 times, aggregating more spaceflights than any other spacecraft as of December 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-Guinness_most_spaceflights-3) The Space Shuttle launch vehicle had three main components: the [Space Shuttle orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter"), a single-use central fuel tank, and two reusable [solid rocket boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_rocket_booster "Solid rocket booster"). Nearly 25,000 [heat-resistant tiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") cover the orbiter to protect it from high temperatures on re-entry.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-4)

_Discovery_ became the third operational orbiter to enter service, preceded by _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ and _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-5) After the _Challenger_ and _Columbia_ accidents, _Discovery_ became the oldest surviving orbiter. It embarked on its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), on February 24, 2011, and touched down for the last time at [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") on March 9,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-6) having spent a cumulative total of nearly a full year in space. _Discovery_ performed both research and [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS) assembly missions, and also carried the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") into orbit among other satellites.

_Discovery_ was the first operational shuttle to be retired, followed by _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ and then _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_. The shuttle is now on display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") of the [Smithsonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")[National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The name _Discovery_ was chosen to carry on a tradition based on ships of exploration,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-ov103-2) primarily [HMS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1774) "HMS Discovery (1774)"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-7) one of the ships commanded by Captain [James Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook "James Cook") during his third and final major voyage from 1776 to 1779, and [Henry Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hudson "Henry Hudson")'s [_Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(1602_ship) "Discovery (1602 ship)"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-ov103-2) which was used in 1610–1611 to explore [Hudson Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay "Hudson Bay") and search for a [Northwest Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Passage "Northwest Passage"). Other ships bearing the name have included [HMS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1874) "HMS Discovery (1874)")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-8) of the 1875–1876 [British Arctic Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Arctic_Expedition "British Arctic Expedition") to the North Pole, and [RRS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RRS_Discovery "RRS Discovery"), which carried the 1901–1904 [_Discovery_ Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Expedition "Discovery Expedition") to [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica "Antarctica"), led by [Captain Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Falcon_Scott "Robert Falcon Scott").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-pao-9)

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launched the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") and conducted the [second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-82 "STS-82") and [third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-103 "STS-103") Hubble service missions. It also launched the [_Ulysses_ probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_probe "Ulysses probe") and three [TDRS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_and_Data_Relay_Satellite_System "Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System") satellites. Twice _Discovery_ was chosen as the "Return To Flight" Orbiter, first in 1988 after the [loss of _Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") in 1986, and then again for the twin "Return To Flight" missions in July 2005 and July 2006 after the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") in 2003. [Project Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury "Project Mercury") astronaut [John Glenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glenn "John Glenn"), who was 77 at the time, flew with _Discovery_ on [STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95") in 1998, making him the oldest person to go into space at that time in history.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-over-10)

Had plans to launch [United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") payloads from [Vandenberg Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Air_Force_Base "Vandenberg Air Force Base") gone ahead, _Discovery_ would have become the dedicated [US Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Air_Force "US Air Force") shuttle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-11) Its first West Coast mission, [STS-62-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-62-A "STS-62-A"), was scheduled for 1986, but [canceled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canceled_Space_Shuttle_missions "Canceled Space Shuttle missions") in the aftermath of the _[Challenger disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger\_disaster "Challenger disaster")_.

On May 27, 1999, _Discovery_ was launched on [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96"), the first shuttle mission to dock with the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-12)

_Discovery_ was retired after completing its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133") on March 9, 2011. The spacecraft is now on display in Virginia at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center"), an annex of the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-nasm-13)

During its construction, _Discovery_ was fitted with several black tiles near the middle starboard window where there should have been white tiles. It is unknown if this was the result of a harmless manufacturing mishap or done intentionally to give a distinctive look to the shuttle. This feature has been called 'teardrop' and allowed _Discovery_ to be told apart from the rest of the fleet without looking at its name, although often unnoticed by the uninitiated.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-14)

The spacecraft weighed roughly 6,870 lb (3,120 kg) less than _Columbia_ when it was brought into service due to optimalizations determined during the construction and testing of _Enterprise_, _Columbia_ and _Challenger_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-over-10)_Discovery_ weighs 6 pounds (2.7 kg) heavier than _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_ and 363 pounds (165 kg) heavier than _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ after further weight-saving adjustments were made.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-FT_facts-15)

Part of the _Discovery_ weight optimizations included the greater use of quilted [AFRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Flexible_Insulation_Blankets/Advanced_Flexible_Reusable_Insulation_(FIB/AFRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") blankets rather than the white [LRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Low-temperature_reusable_surface_insulation_(LRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") tiles on the fuselage, and the use of [graphite epoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphite_epoxy "Graphite epoxy") instead of aluminum for the payload bay doors and some of the wing spars and beams.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-16)

Upon its delivery to the Kennedy Space Center in 1983, _Discovery_ was modified alongside _Challenger_ to accommodate the liquid-fueled [Centaur-G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centaur-G "Centaur-G") booster, which had been planned for use beginning in 1986 but was cancelled in the wake of the _Challenger_ disaster.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-17)

Beginning in late 1995, the orbiter underwent a nine-month Orbiter Maintenance Down Period (OMDP) in [Palmdale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmdale,_California "Palmdale, California"). This included outfitting the vehicle with a fifth set of cryogenic tanks and an external airlock to support missions to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"). As with all the orbiters, it could be attached to the top of specialized aircraft and did so in June 1996 when it returned to the Kennedy Space Center, and later in April 2012 when sent to the Udvar-Hazy Center, riding [piggy-back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piggy-back_(transportation) "Piggy-back (transportation)") on a [modified Boeing 747](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-over-10)

After [STS-105](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-105 "STS-105"), _Discovery_ became the first of the orbiter fleet to undergo Orbiter Major Modification (OMM) period at the Kennedy Space Center. Work began in September 2002 to prepare the vehicle for Return to Flight. The work included scheduled upgrades and additional safety modifications.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-over-10)

_Discovery_ was [decommissioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_decommissioning "Ship decommissioning") on March 9, 2011.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-manifest-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-CSCS1-20) NASA offered _Discovery_ to the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum") for public display and preservation, after a month-long [decontamination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contamination_control "Contamination control") process,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-21) as part of the national collection.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-smithsonian-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-smithsonian-houston-chronical-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-24)_Discovery_ replaced [_Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise"), which was in the Smithsonian's display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") until 2011.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-27)_Discovery_ was transported to [Washington Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Dulles_International_Airport "Washington Dulles International Airport") on April 17, 2012, and was transferred to the Udvar-Hazy Center on April 19 where a welcome ceremony was held. Afterwards, at around 5:30 pm, _Discovery_ was rolled to its "final wheels stop" in the Udvar-Hazy Center.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-29)

Texas senators [John Cornyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cornyn "John Cornyn") and [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz "Ted Cruz") added a provision to the 2025 [One Big Beautiful Bill Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act "One Big Beautiful Bill Act") to spend $85 million to relocate a space vehicle that has flown astronauts into space, presumably _Discovery_ because of the sponsors of the provision and previous legislation attempts, from the Udvar-Hazy Center to the [Space Center Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Center_Houston "Space Center Houston") Museum in Texas.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-31) While the Smithsonian estimated that the total cost of the transfer would be approximately $325 million, they also countered that ownership of the shuttle had been transferred to the museum and was no longer federal property, and that Congress did not have the ability to force a transfer.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-33)

## Flights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Flights")]

By its last mission, _Discovery_ had flown 149 million mi (240 million km) in 39 missions, completed 5,830 orbits, and spent 365 days in orbit over 27 years.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-slt-34)_Discovery_ flew [more flights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Orbiter#Flight_statistics "Space Shuttle Orbiter") than any other Orbiter Shuttle, including four in 1985 alone. _Discovery_ flew both "return to flight" missions after the _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger\_Disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger Disaster")_ and _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia\_Disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster")_ disasters: [STS-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26 "STS-26") in 1988, [STS-114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114") in 2005, and [STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121") in 2006. _Discovery_ flew the ante-penultimate mission of the Space Shuttle program, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), having launched on February 24, 2011. _Endeavour_ flew [STS-134](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-134 "STS-134") and _Atlantis_ performed [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135"), NASA's last Space Shuttle mission. On February 24, 2011, Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launched from Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39-A to begin its final orbital flight.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-ares6-35)

## Flow directors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Flow directors")]

The Flow Director was responsible for the overall preparation of the shuttle for launch and processing it after landing, and remained permanently assigned to head the spacecraft's ground crew while the astronaut flight crews changed for every mission. Each shuttle's Flow Director was supported by a Vehicle Manager for the same spacecraft. Space Shuttle _Discovery'_ s Flow Directors were:

*   Until 01/1991: John J. "Tip" Talone Jr. (afterwards Flow Director for _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-science.ksc.nasa.gov-38)
*   01/1991 – 09/1992: John C. "Chris" Fairey[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-science.ksc.nasa.gov-38)
*   09/1992 – 10/1996: [David A. King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_A._King_(engineer) "David A. King (engineer)")[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-39)
*   10/1996 – 05/2000: W. Scott Cilento[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-40)
*   12/2000 – 03/2011: Stephanie S. Stilson[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-41)

**Space Shuttle _Discovery_** ([Orbiter Vehicle Designation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orbiter_Vehicle_Designation "Orbiter Vehicle Designation"): **OV-103**) is a retired American [Space Shuttle orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter"). The [spaceplane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spaceplane "Spaceplane") was one of the [orbiters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter") from [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program") and the third of five fully operational orbiters to be built.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-ov103-2) Its first mission, [STS-41-D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D "STS-41-D"), flew from August 30 to September 5, 1984. Over 27 years of service it launched and landed 39 times, aggregating more spaceflights than any other spacecraft as of December 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-Guinness_most_spaceflights-3) The Space Shuttle launch vehicle had three main components: the [Space Shuttle orbiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_orbiter "Space Shuttle orbiter"), a single-use central fuel tank, and two reusable [solid rocket boosters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solid_rocket_booster "Solid rocket booster"). Nearly 25,000 [heat-resistant tiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") cover the orbiter to protect it from high temperatures on re-entry.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-4)

_Discovery_ became the third operational orbiter to enter service, preceded by _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia "Space Shuttle Columbia")_ and _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger "Space Shuttle Challenger")_.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-5) After the _Challenger_ and _Columbia_ accidents, _Discovery_ became the oldest surviving orbiter. It embarked on its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), on February 24, 2011, and touched down for the last time at [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center") on March 9,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-6) having spent a cumulative total of nearly a full year in space. _Discovery_ performed both research and [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS) assembly missions, and also carried the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") into orbit among other satellites.

_Discovery_ was the first operational shuttle to be retired, followed by _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ and then _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_. The shuttle is now on display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") of the [Smithsonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")[National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The name _Discovery_ was chosen to carry on a tradition based on ships of exploration,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-ov103-2) primarily [HMS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1774) "HMS Discovery (1774)"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-7) one of the ships commanded by Captain [James Cook](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Cook "James Cook") during his third and final major voyage from 1776 to 1779, and [Henry Hudson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hudson "Henry Hudson")'s [_Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_(1602_ship) "Discovery (1602 ship)"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-ov103-2) which was used in 1610–1611 to explore [Hudson Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hudson_Bay "Hudson Bay") and search for a [Northwest Passage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwest_Passage "Northwest Passage"). Other ships bearing the name have included [HMS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HMS_Discovery_(1874) "HMS Discovery (1874)")[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-8) of the 1875–1876 [British Arctic Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Arctic_Expedition "British Arctic Expedition") to the North Pole, and [RRS _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RRS_Discovery "RRS Discovery"), which carried the 1901–1904 [_Discovery_ Expedition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discovery_Expedition "Discovery Expedition") to [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica "Antarctica"), led by [Captain Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Falcon_Scott "Robert Falcon Scott").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-pao-9)

Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launched the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") and conducted the [second](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-82 "STS-82") and [third](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-103 "STS-103") Hubble service missions. It also launched the [_Ulysses_ probe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulysses_probe "Ulysses probe") and three [TDRS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracking_and_Data_Relay_Satellite_System "Tracking and Data Relay Satellite System") satellites. Twice _Discovery_ was chosen as the "Return To Flight" Orbiter, first in 1988 after the [loss of _Challenger_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster") in 1986, and then again for the twin "Return To Flight" missions in July 2005 and July 2006 after the [_Columbia_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Columbia_disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia disaster") in 2003. [Project Mercury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Mercury "Project Mercury") astronaut [John Glenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glenn "John Glenn"), who was 77 at the time, flew with _Discovery_ on [STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95") in 1998, making him the oldest person to go into space at that time in history.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-over-10)

Had plans to launch [United States Department of Defense](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") payloads from [Vandenberg Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vandenberg_Air_Force_Base "Vandenberg Air Force Base") gone ahead, _Discovery_ would have become the dedicated [US Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Air_Force "US Air Force") shuttle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-11) Its first West Coast mission, [STS-62-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-62-A "STS-62-A"), was scheduled for 1986, but [canceled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canceled_Space_Shuttle_missions "Canceled Space Shuttle missions") in the aftermath of the _[Challenger disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger\_disaster "Challenger disaster")_.

On May 27, 1999, _Discovery_ was launched on [STS-96](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-96 "STS-96"), the first shuttle mission to dock with the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-12)

_Discovery_ was retired after completing its final mission, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133") on March 9, 2011. The spacecraft is now on display in Virginia at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center"), an annex of the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-nasm-13)

During its construction, _Discovery_ was fitted with several black tiles near the middle starboard window where there should have been white tiles. It is unknown if this was the result of a harmless manufacturing mishap or done intentionally to give a distinctive look to the shuttle. This feature has been called 'teardrop' and allowed _Discovery_ to be told apart from the rest of the fleet without looking at its name, although often unnoticed by the uninitiated.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-14)

The spacecraft weighed roughly 6,870 lb (3,120 kg) less than _Columbia_ when it was brought into service due to optimalizations determined during the construction and testing of _Enterprise_, _Columbia_ and _Challenger_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-over-10)_Discovery_ weighs 6 pounds (2.7 kg) heavier than _[Atlantis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis")_ and 363 pounds (165 kg) heavier than _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ after further weight-saving adjustments were made.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-FT_facts-15)

Part of the _Discovery_ weight optimizations included the greater use of quilted [AFRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Flexible_Insulation_Blankets/Advanced_Flexible_Reusable_Insulation_(FIB/AFRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") blankets rather than the white [LRSI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_thermal_protection_system#Low-temperature_reusable_surface_insulation_(LRSI) "Space Shuttle thermal protection system") tiles on the fuselage, and the use of [graphite epoxy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphite_epoxy "Graphite epoxy") instead of aluminum for the payload bay doors and some of the wing spars and beams.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-16)

Upon its delivery to the Kennedy Space Center in 1983, _Discovery_ was modified alongside _Challenger_ to accommodate the liquid-fueled [Centaur-G](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centaur-G "Centaur-G") booster, which had been planned for use beginning in 1986 but was cancelled in the wake of the _Challenger_ disaster.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-17)

Beginning in late 1995, the orbiter underwent a nine-month Orbiter Maintenance Down Period (OMDP) in [Palmdale, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmdale,_California "Palmdale, California"). This included outfitting the vehicle with a fifth set of cryogenic tanks and an external airlock to support missions to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"). As with all the orbiters, it could be attached to the top of specialized aircraft and did so in June 1996 when it returned to the Kennedy Space Center, and later in April 2012 when sent to the Udvar-Hazy Center, riding [piggy-back](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piggy-back_(transportation) "Piggy-back (transportation)") on a [modified Boeing 747](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle_Carrier_Aircraft "Shuttle Carrier Aircraft").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-over-10)

After [STS-105](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-105 "STS-105"), _Discovery_ became the first of the orbiter fleet to undergo Orbiter Major Modification (OMM) period at the Kennedy Space Center. Work began in September 2002 to prepare the vehicle for Return to Flight. The work included scheduled upgrades and additional safety modifications.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-over-10)

_Discovery_ was [decommissioned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ship_decommissioning "Ship decommissioning") on March 9, 2011.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-manifest-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-CSCS1-20) NASA offered _Discovery_ to the [Smithsonian Institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithsonian_Institution "Smithsonian Institution")'s [National Air and Space Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Air_and_Space_Museum "National Air and Space Museum") for public display and preservation, after a month-long [decontamination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contamination_control "Contamination control") process,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-21) as part of the national collection.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-smithsonian-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-smithsonian-houston-chronical-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-24)_Discovery_ replaced [_Enterprise_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Enterprise "Space Shuttle Enterprise"), which was in the Smithsonian's display at the [Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_F._Udvar-Hazy_Center "Steven F. Udvar-Hazy Center") until 2011.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-27)_Discovery_ was transported to [Washington Dulles International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Dulles_International_Airport "Washington Dulles International Airport") on April 17, 2012, and was transferred to the Udvar-Hazy Center on April 19 where a welcome ceremony was held. Afterwards, at around 5:30 pm, _Discovery_ was rolled to its "final wheels stop" in the Udvar-Hazy Center.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-29)

Texas senators [John Cornyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cornyn "John Cornyn") and [Ted Cruz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ted_Cruz "Ted Cruz") added a provision to the 2025 [One Big Beautiful Bill Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_Big_Beautiful_Bill_Act "One Big Beautiful Bill Act") to spend $85 million to relocate a space vehicle that has flown astronauts into space, presumably _Discovery_ because of the sponsors of the provision and previous legislation attempts, from the Udvar-Hazy Center to the [Space Center Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Center_Houston "Space Center Houston") Museum in Texas.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-31) While the Smithsonian estimated that the total cost of the transfer would be approximately $325 million, they also countered that ownership of the shuttle had been transferred to the museum and was no longer federal property, and that Congress did not have the ability to force a transfer.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-33)

## Flights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Flights")]

By its last mission, _Discovery_ had flown 149 million mi (240 million km) in 39 missions, completed 5,830 orbits, and spent 365 days in orbit over 27 years.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-slt-34)_Discovery_ flew [more flights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Orbiter#Flight_statistics "Space Shuttle Orbiter") than any other Orbiter Shuttle, including four in 1985 alone. _Discovery_ flew both "return to flight" missions after the _[Challenger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Challenger\_Disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger Disaster")_ and _[Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Columbia\_Disaster "Space Shuttle Columbia Disaster")_ disasters: [STS-26](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-26 "STS-26") in 1988, [STS-114](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-114 "STS-114") in 2005, and [STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121") in 2006. _Discovery_ flew the ante-penultimate mission of the Space Shuttle program, [STS-133](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-133 "STS-133"), having launched on February 24, 2011. _Endeavour_ flew [STS-134](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-134 "STS-134") and _Atlantis_ performed [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135"), NASA's last Space Shuttle mission. On February 24, 2011, Space Shuttle _Discovery_ launched from Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39-A to begin its final orbital flight.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-ares6-35)

## Flow directors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Space_Shuttle_Discovery&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Flow directors")]

The Flow Director was responsible for the overall preparation of the shuttle for launch and processing it after landing, and remained permanently assigned to head the spacecraft's ground crew while the astronaut flight crews changed for every mission. Each shuttle's Flow Director was supported by a Vehicle Manager for the same spacecraft. Space Shuttle _Discovery'_ s Flow Directors were:

*   Until 01/1991: John J. "Tip" Talone Jr. (afterwards Flow Director for _[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-science.ksc.nasa.gov-38)
*   01/1991 – 09/1992: John C. "Chris" Fairey[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-science.ksc.nasa.gov-38)
*   09/1992 – 10/1996: [David A. King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_A._King_(engineer) "David A. King (engineer)")[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-39)
*   10/1996 – 05/2000: W. Scott Cilento[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-40)
*   12/2000 – 03/2011: Stephanie S. Stilson[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery#cite_note-41)

This is a list of persons who served aboard **Space Shuttles**, arranged in chronological order by [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") missions.

Abbreviations:

*   **PC** = Payload Commander
*   **MSE** = [USAF Manned Spaceflight Engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manned_Spaceflight_Engineer_Program "Manned Spaceflight Engineer Program")
*   **Mir** = Launched to be part of the crew of the [Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir") Space Station
*   **ISS** = Launched to be part of the crew of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").

Names of astronauts returning from the Mir or ISS on the Space Shuttle are shown in _italics_. They did not have specific crew roles, but are listed in the Payload Specialist columns for reasons of space.

Only two flights have carried more than seven crew members for either launch or landing. [STS-61-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-A "STS-61-A") in 1985 is the only flight to have both launched and landed with a crew of eight, and [STS-71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-71 "STS-71") in 1995 is the only other flight to have landed with a crew of eight.

This is a list of persons who served aboard **Space Shuttles**, arranged in chronological order by [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") missions.

Abbreviations:

*   **PC** = Payload Commander
*   **MSE** = [USAF Manned Spaceflight Engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manned_Spaceflight_Engineer_Program "Manned Spaceflight Engineer Program")
*   **Mir** = Launched to be part of the crew of the [Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir") Space Station
*   **ISS** = Launched to be part of the crew of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").

Names of astronauts returning from the Mir or ISS on the Space Shuttle are shown in _italics_. They did not have specific crew roles, but are listed in the Payload Specialist columns for reasons of space.

Only two flights have carried more than seven crew members for either launch or landing. [STS-61-A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-61-A "STS-61-A") in 1985 is the only flight to have both launched and landed with a crew of eight, and [STS-71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-71 "STS-71") in 1995 is the only other flight to have landed with a crew of eight.

**STS-41-D** (formerly STS-14) was the 12th flight of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), and the maiden flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_. It was launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on August 30, 1984, and landed at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), on September 5, 1984. Three commercial [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite") were deployed into orbit during the six-day mission, and a number of scientific experiments were conducted, including a prototype [extendable solar array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_system_of_the_International_Space_Station "Electrical system of the International Space Station") that would eventually form the basis of the main solar arrays on the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS).

The mission was delayed by more than two months from its original planned launch date, having experienced the Space Shuttle program's first launch abort at T−4 seconds on June 26, 1984.

## Mission background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission background")]

The launch was originally planned for June 25, 1984, but because of a variety of technical problems, including rollback to the [Vehicle Assembly Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_Assembly_Building "Vehicle Assembly Building") (VAB) to replace a faulty [Space Shuttle Main Engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Main_Engine "Space Shuttle Main Engine") (SSME), the launch was delayed by over two months. The June 26, 1984, launch attempt marked the first time since [Gemini 6A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemini_6A "Gemini 6A") that a crewed spacecraft had experienced a shutdown of its engines just prior to launch.

### June 1984 launch attempt

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: June 1984 launch attempt")]

During the June 26, 1984, launch attempt, there was a launch abort at T−4 seconds, followed by a pad fire about ten minutes later.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-STS-41-4) Because the center engine had not started when the abort was triggered, confusion ensued as the [flight controllers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_controller "Flight controller") were unable to verify its state:

> Commentary: "We have a cut off".  
>  "NTD [_NASA Test Director_] we have a RSLS [_Redundant Set Launch Sequencer_] abort".
> 
> 
> Commentary: "We have an abort by the onboard computers of the orbiter Discovery".  
>  "Break break, break break, GLS [_Ground Launch Sequencer_] shows engine one not shut down".  
>  "OK, PLT [_pilot_]?"  
>  "CSME [_Space Shuttle Main Engines_] verify engine one".  
>  "You want me to shut down engine one?"  
>  "We do not show engine start on one".  
>  "OTC [_Orbiter test conductor_] I can verify shutdown on verify on engine one, we haven't start prepped engine one".  
>  "All engines shut down I can verify that".
> 
> 
> Commentary: "We can now verify all three engines have been shut down".  
>  "We have red lights on engines two and three in the cockpit, not on one".  
>  "All right, CSME verify engine one safe for APU [_[auxiliary power unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary\_power\_unit "Auxiliary power unit")_] shutdown".  
>  "If I can verify that?"  
>  "OTC GPC [_General Purpose Computer_] go for APU shutdown".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-5)

Mission Specialist Steve Hawley was reported as saying following the abort: "Gee, I thought we'd be a lot higher at MECO (Main Engine Cut-Off)!".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-autogenerated1-6) About ten minutes later, the following was heard on live TV coverage:

> "We have indication two of our fire detectors on the zero level; no response. They're side by side right next to the engine area. The engineer requested that we turn on the heat shield fire water which is what could be seen spraying up in the vicinity of the engine bells of _Discovery_'s three main engines".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-7)

While evacuating the shuttle 20 minutes later, the crew was doused with water from the pad deluge system, which was activated due to a hydrogen fire on the launch pad caused by the free hydrogen (fuel) that had collected around the engine nozzles following the shutdown and engine anomaly.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-8) Because the fire was invisible to humans, had the astronauts used the normal emergency escape procedure across the service arm to the slidewire escape baskets, they would have run into the fire.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-walker20050317-9)

Changes to procedures resulting from the abort included more practicing of "safing" the orbiter following aborts at various points, the use of the fire suppression system in all pad aborts, and the testing of the slidewire escape system with a real person ([Charles F. Bolden Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Bolden "Charles Bolden")). It emerged that launch controllers were reluctant to order the crew to evacuate during the STS-41-D abort, as the slidewire had not been ridden by a human.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-autogenerated1-6)

Examination of telemetry data indicated that the engine malfunction had been caused by a stuck valve that prevented proper flow of LOX into the combustion chamber.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

STS-41-D launched at 08:41:50 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on August 30, 1984, after a six-minute, fifty-second delay when a private aircraft flew into the restricted airspace near the launch pad. It was the fourth launch attempt for _Discovery_. Because of the two-month delay, the [STS-41-F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canceled_Space_Shuttle_missions "Canceled Space Shuttle missions") mission was canceled (STS-41-E had already been canceled), and its primary payloads were included on the STS-41-D flight. The combined cargo weighed over 18,681 kg (41,185 lb), a record for a Space Shuttle payload up to that time.

The six-person flight crew consisted of [Henry W. Hartsfield Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_W._Hartsfield_Jr. "Henry W. Hartsfield Jr."), commander, making his second shuttle mission; pilot [Michael L. Coats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Coats "Michael Coats"); three mission specialists – [Judith A. Resnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Resnik "Judith Resnik"), [Richard M. Mullane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Mullane "Mike Mullane") and [Steven A. Hawley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Hawley "Steven Hawley"); and a payload specialist, [Charles D. Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_D._Walker "Charles D. Walker"), an employee of [McDonnell Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonnell_Douglas "McDonnell Douglas"). Walker was the first commercially sponsored payload specialist to fly aboard the Space Shuttle. Resnik became the second American woman to fly any NASA space mission, after [Sally K. Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Ride "Sally Ride").

Primary cargo of _Discovery_ consisted of three commercial [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite"): SBS-4 for [Satellite Business Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_Business_Systems "Satellite Business Systems"), [Telstar 302](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telstar_302 "Telstar 302") for [Telesat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telesat "Telesat") of [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), and [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-2, or [Leasat-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom"), a [Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hughes_Aircraft_Company "Hughes Aircraft Company")-built satellite leased to the [U.S. Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy"); all three were Hughes-built satellites. Leasat-2 was the first large communications satellite designed specifically to be deployed from the Space Shuttle. All three satellites were deployed successfully and became operational.

Another payload was the OAST-1 [solar array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaic_module "Photovoltaic module"), a device 4 m (13 ft) wide and 31 m (102 ft) high, which folded into a package 18 cm (7.1 in) deep. The array carried a number of different types of experimental [solar cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cell "Solar cell") and was extended to its full height several times during the mission. At the time, it was the largest structure ever extended from a crewed spacecraft, and it demonstrated the feasibility of large lightweight solar arrays for use on future orbital installations, such as the International Space Station (ISS).

The McDonnell Douglas-sponsored Continuous Flow Electrophoresis System (CFES) experiment, using living cells, was more elaborate than the one flown on previous missions, and payload specialist Walker operated it for more than 100 hours during the flight. A student experiment to study [crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal "Crystal") growth in [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment") was also carried out. The highlights of the mission were filmed using an [IMAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMAX "IMAX")[motion picture camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movie_camera "Movie camera"), and later appeared in the 1985 documentary film _[The Dream is Alive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dream\_is\_Alive "The Dream is Alive")_. On September 3, 1984, concern arose over the formation of ice on the waste dump nozzle of the shuttle. The cause was an obstruction in the shuttle's external wastewater dumping system that caused a 61 cm (24 in) "[pee-sicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urine "Urine")" to form during the mission; Hartsfield removed it with the Remote Manipulator System ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")) the following day.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-walker20050414-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-11)

The mission lasted 6 days, 0 hour, 56 minutes, and 4 seconds, with landing taking place on Runway 17 at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") at 06:37:54 a.m. PDT on September 5, 1984. During STS-41-D, _Discovery_ traveled a total of 4,010,000 km (2,490,000 mi) and made 97 orbits. The orbiter was transported back to KSC on September 10, 1984. Ominously, STS-41-D was the first Shuttle mission in which blow-by damage to the SRB O-rings was discovered, with a small amount of soot found beyond the primary O-ring. Following the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"), [Morton Thiokol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiokol "Thiokol") engineer Brian Russell called this finding the first "big red flag" on SRB Joint and O-ring safety.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-12)

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

The 12 stars within the blue field indicate the flight's original numerical designation as STS-12 in the Space Transportation System's mission sequence. A representation of _Discovery's_ namesake is manifested in a sailing ship, which is linked to the Shuttle (with the OAST solar array in the payload bay) via a red, white, and blue path, signifying its maiden voyage.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-chronology-16)

**STS-41-D** (formerly STS-14) was the 12th flight of [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")'s [Space Shuttle program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_program "Space Shuttle program"), and the maiden flight of Space Shuttle _Discovery_. It was launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on August 30, 1984, and landed at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), on September 5, 1984. Three commercial [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite") were deployed into orbit during the six-day mission, and a number of scientific experiments were conducted, including a prototype [extendable solar array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electrical_system_of_the_International_Space_Station "Electrical system of the International Space Station") that would eventually form the basis of the main solar arrays on the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") (ISS).

The mission was delayed by more than two months from its original planned launch date, having experienced the Space Shuttle program's first launch abort at T−4 seconds on June 26, 1984.

## Mission background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Mission background")]

The launch was originally planned for June 25, 1984, but because of a variety of technical problems, including rollback to the [Vehicle Assembly Building](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vehicle_Assembly_Building "Vehicle Assembly Building") (VAB) to replace a faulty [Space Shuttle Main Engine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Main_Engine "Space Shuttle Main Engine") (SSME), the launch was delayed by over two months. The June 26, 1984, launch attempt marked the first time since [Gemini 6A](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gemini_6A "Gemini 6A") that a crewed spacecraft had experienced a shutdown of its engines just prior to launch.

### June 1984 launch attempt

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: June 1984 launch attempt")]

During the June 26, 1984, launch attempt, there was a launch abort at T−4 seconds, followed by a pad fire about ten minutes later.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-STS-41-4) Because the center engine had not started when the abort was triggered, confusion ensued as the [flight controllers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_controller "Flight controller") were unable to verify its state:

> Commentary: "We have a cut off".  
>  "NTD [_NASA Test Director_] we have a RSLS [_Redundant Set Launch Sequencer_] abort".
> 
> 
> Commentary: "We have an abort by the onboard computers of the orbiter Discovery".  
>  "Break break, break break, GLS [_Ground Launch Sequencer_] shows engine one not shut down".  
>  "OK, PLT [_pilot_]?"  
>  "CSME [_Space Shuttle Main Engines_] verify engine one".  
>  "You want me to shut down engine one?"  
>  "We do not show engine start on one".  
>  "OTC [_Orbiter test conductor_] I can verify shutdown on verify on engine one, we haven't start prepped engine one".  
>  "All engines shut down I can verify that".
> 
> 
> Commentary: "We can now verify all three engines have been shut down".  
>  "We have red lights on engines two and three in the cockpit, not on one".  
>  "All right, CSME verify engine one safe for APU [_[auxiliary power unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auxiliary\_power\_unit "Auxiliary power unit")_] shutdown".  
>  "If I can verify that?"  
>  "OTC GPC [_General Purpose Computer_] go for APU shutdown".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-5)

Mission Specialist Steve Hawley was reported as saying following the abort: "Gee, I thought we'd be a lot higher at MECO (Main Engine Cut-Off)!".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-autogenerated1-6) About ten minutes later, the following was heard on live TV coverage:

> "We have indication two of our fire detectors on the zero level; no response. They're side by side right next to the engine area. The engineer requested that we turn on the heat shield fire water which is what could be seen spraying up in the vicinity of the engine bells of _Discovery_'s three main engines".[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-7)

While evacuating the shuttle 20 minutes later, the crew was doused with water from the pad deluge system, which was activated due to a hydrogen fire on the launch pad caused by the free hydrogen (fuel) that had collected around the engine nozzles following the shutdown and engine anomaly.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-8) Because the fire was invisible to humans, had the astronauts used the normal emergency escape procedure across the service arm to the slidewire escape baskets, they would have run into the fire.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-walker20050317-9)

Changes to procedures resulting from the abort included more practicing of "safing" the orbiter following aborts at various points, the use of the fire suppression system in all pad aborts, and the testing of the slidewire escape system with a real person ([Charles F. Bolden Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Bolden "Charles Bolden")). It emerged that launch controllers were reluctant to order the crew to evacuate during the STS-41-D abort, as the slidewire had not been ridden by a human.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-autogenerated1-6)

Examination of telemetry data indicated that the engine malfunction had been caused by a stuck valve that prevented proper flow of LOX into the combustion chamber.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Mission summary

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Mission summary")]

STS-41-D launched at 08:41:50 a.m. [EDT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Time_Zone "Eastern Time Zone") on August 30, 1984, after a six-minute, fifty-second delay when a private aircraft flew into the restricted airspace near the launch pad. It was the fourth launch attempt for _Discovery_. Because of the two-month delay, the [STS-41-F](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canceled_Space_Shuttle_missions "Canceled Space Shuttle missions") mission was canceled (STS-41-E had already been canceled), and its primary payloads were included on the STS-41-D flight. The combined cargo weighed over 18,681 kg (41,185 lb), a record for a Space Shuttle payload up to that time.

The six-person flight crew consisted of [Henry W. Hartsfield Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_W._Hartsfield_Jr. "Henry W. Hartsfield Jr."), commander, making his second shuttle mission; pilot [Michael L. Coats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Coats "Michael Coats"); three mission specialists – [Judith A. Resnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judith_Resnik "Judith Resnik"), [Richard M. Mullane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Mullane "Mike Mullane") and [Steven A. Hawley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Hawley "Steven Hawley"); and a payload specialist, [Charles D. Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_D._Walker "Charles D. Walker"), an employee of [McDonnell Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonnell_Douglas "McDonnell Douglas"). Walker was the first commercially sponsored payload specialist to fly aboard the Space Shuttle. Resnik became the second American woman to fly any NASA space mission, after [Sally K. Ride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Ride "Sally Ride").

Primary cargo of _Discovery_ consisted of three commercial [communications satellites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_satellite "Communications satellite"): SBS-4 for [Satellite Business Systems](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Satellite_Business_Systems "Satellite Business Systems"), [Telstar 302](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telstar_302 "Telstar 302") for [Telesat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telesat "Telesat") of [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada "Canada"), and [Syncom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom") IV-2, or [Leasat-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syncom "Syncom"), a [Hughes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hughes_Aircraft_Company "Hughes Aircraft Company")-built satellite leased to the [U.S. Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Navy "United States Navy"); all three were Hughes-built satellites. Leasat-2 was the first large communications satellite designed specifically to be deployed from the Space Shuttle. All three satellites were deployed successfully and became operational.

Another payload was the OAST-1 [solar array](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photovoltaic_module "Photovoltaic module"), a device 4 m (13 ft) wide and 31 m (102 ft) high, which folded into a package 18 cm (7.1 in) deep. The array carried a number of different types of experimental [solar cells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cell "Solar cell") and was extended to its full height several times during the mission. At the time, it was the largest structure ever extended from a crewed spacecraft, and it demonstrated the feasibility of large lightweight solar arrays for use on future orbital installations, such as the International Space Station (ISS).

The McDonnell Douglas-sponsored Continuous Flow Electrophoresis System (CFES) experiment, using living cells, was more elaborate than the one flown on previous missions, and payload specialist Walker operated it for more than 100 hours during the flight. A student experiment to study [crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal "Crystal") growth in [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micro-g_environment "Micro-g environment") was also carried out. The highlights of the mission were filmed using an [IMAX](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IMAX "IMAX")[motion picture camera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movie_camera "Movie camera"), and later appeared in the 1985 documentary film _[The Dream is Alive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Dream\_is\_Alive "The Dream is Alive")_. On September 3, 1984, concern arose over the formation of ice on the waste dump nozzle of the shuttle. The cause was an obstruction in the shuttle's external wastewater dumping system that caused a 61 cm (24 in) "[pee-sicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urine "Urine")" to form during the mission; Hartsfield removed it with the Remote Manipulator System ([Canadarm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadarm "Canadarm")) the following day.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-walker20050414-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-11)

The mission lasted 6 days, 0 hour, 56 minutes, and 4 seconds, with landing taking place on Runway 17 at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base") at 06:37:54 a.m. PDT on September 5, 1984. During STS-41-D, _Discovery_ traveled a total of 4,010,000 km (2,490,000 mi) and made 97 orbits. The orbiter was transported back to KSC on September 10, 1984. Ominously, STS-41-D was the first Shuttle mission in which blow-by damage to the SRB O-rings was discovered, with a small amount of soot found beyond the primary O-ring. Following the [_Challenger_ disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Challenger_disaster "Space Shuttle Challenger disaster"), [Morton Thiokol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiokol "Thiokol") engineer Brian Russell called this finding the first "big red flag" on SRB Joint and O-ring safety.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-12)

## Mission insignia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Mission insignia")]

The 12 stars within the blue field indicate the flight's original numerical designation as STS-12 in the Space Transportation System's mission sequence. A representation of _Discovery's_ namesake is manifested in a sailing ship, which is linked to the Shuttle (with the OAST solar array in the payload bay) via a red, white, and blue path, signifying its maiden voyage.

## Wake-up calls

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=STS-41-D&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Wake-up calls")]

NASA began a tradition of playing music to astronauts during the [Project Gemini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_Gemini "Project Gemini"), and first used music to wake up a flight crew during [Apollo 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_15 "Apollo 15"). Each track is specially chosen, often by the astronauts' families, and usually has a special meaning to an individual member of the crew, or is applicable to their daily activities.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-41-D#cite_note-chronology-16)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
For Soviet Space Shuttle missions, see List of Buran missions.
Launch of Space Shuttle Columbia on 12 April 1981 at Pad 39A for mission STS-1

The Space Shuttle was a partially reusable low Earth orbital spacecraft system operated by NASA (the National Aeronautics and Space Administration). Its official program name was Space Transportation System (STS), taken from a 1969 plan for a system of reusable spacecraft of which it was the only item funded for development.[1] Operational missions launched numerous satellites, conducted science experiments in orbit, and participated in construction and servicing of the International Space Station (ISS). The first of four orbital test flights occurred in 1981, leading to operational flights beginning in 1982.

From 1981 to 2011 a total of 135 missions were flown, all launched from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. During that time period the fleet logged 1,322 days, 19 hours, 21 minutes and 23 seconds of flight time.[2] The longest orbital flight of the Shuttle was STS-80 at 17 days 15 hours, while the shortest flight was STS-51-L at one minute 13 seconds when the Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart during launch. The cold morning shrank an O-ring on the right solid rocket booster causing the external fuel tank to explode. The shuttles docked with Russian space station Mir nine times and visited the ISS thirty-seven times. The highest altitude (apogee) achieved by the shuttle was 386 mi (621 km) when deploying the Hubble Space Telescope.[3] The program flew a total of 355 people representing 16 countries, and with 852 total shuttle fliers.[4] The Kennedy Space Center served as the landing site for 78 missions, while 54 missions landed at Edwards Air Force Base in California and one mission landed at White Sands, New Mexico.[5]

The first orbiter built, Enterprise, was used for atmospheric flight tests (ALT) but future plans to upgrade it to orbital capability were ultimately canceled. Four fully operational orbiters were initially built: Columbia, Challenger, Discovery, and Atlantis. Challenger and Columbia were destroyed in mission accidents in 1986 and 2003 respectively, killing a total of fourteen astronauts. A fifth operational orbiter, Endeavour, was built in 1991 to replace Challenger. The Space Shuttle was retired from service upon the conclusion of STS-135 by Atlantis on 21 July 2011.[6]

Flight numberingedit
Profiles of all five orbiters at launch.

The U.S. Space Shuttle program was officially referred to as the Space Transportation System (STS). Specific shuttle missions were therefore designated with the prefix "STS".[2] Initially, the launches were given sequential numbers indicating order of launch, such as STS-7. Subsequent to the Apollo 13 mishap, due to Administrator of NASA James M. Beggs's triskaidekaphobia and consequent unwillingness to number a forthcoming flight as STS-13,[7][8][9][10] beginning in 1984, each mission was assigned a code, such as STS-41-B, with the first digit (or pair of digits for years 1990 and beyond) indicating the federal fiscal year offset into the program (so 41-B was scheduled for FY 1984, 51-A through 51-L originally for FY 1985, and the third flight in FY 1985 would have been named 51-C), the second digit indicating the launch site (1 was Kennedy Space Center and 2 was Space Launch Complex 6 at Vandenberg Air Force Base, although Vandenberg was never used), and the letter indicating scheduling sequence.[11] These codes were assigned when the launches were initially scheduled and were not changed as missions were delayed or rescheduled.[6] The codes were adopted from STS-41-B through STS-51-L (although the highest code used was actually STS-61-C), and the sequential numbers were used internally at NASA on all processing paperwork.

After the Challenger disaster, NASA returned to using a sequential numbering system, with the number counting from the beginning of the STS program. Unlike the initial system, however, the numbers were assigned based on the initial mission schedule, and did not always reflect actual launch order. This numbering scheme started at 26, with the first flight as STS-26R—the R suffix stood for "reflight" to disambiguate from prior missions. The suffix was used for two years through STS-33R, then the R was dropped.[6] As a result of the changes in systems, flights under different numbering systems could have the same number with one having a letter appended, e.g. flight STS-51 (a mission carried out by Discovery in 1993) was many years after STS-51-A (Discovery's second flight in 1984).[6] It wasn't until STS-127 in 2009 where the flight numbering system returned to a standard and consistent order.

Shuttle missionsedit
Canceled missionsedit
Main article: Canceled Space Shuttle missions

One initial RTLS abort sub-orbital test mission was canceled due to high risk. Many other planned missions were canceled due to the late development of the shuttle, and the Challenger and Columbia disasters.

Four missions were cut short by a day or more while in orbit: STS-2 (equipment failure),[22] STS-35 (weather),[102] STS-44 (equipment failure),[193] and STS-83 (equipment failure, relaunched as STS-94).[193]

Contingency missionsedit
Atlantis and Endeavour on LC-39A and LC-39B. Endeavour was slated to launch for STS-400 rescue mission should Atlantis (STS-125) be found unable to return safely to Earth.
Main article: STS-3xx

STS-300 was the designation for the Space Shuttle Launch on Need (LON) missions to be launched on short notice for STS-114 and STS-121, in the event that the shuttle became disabled or damaged and could not safely return to Earth.[300][301][302] The rescue flight for STS-115, if needed, would have been STS-301. After STS-115, the rescue mission designations were based on the corresponding regular mission that would be replaced should the rescue mission be needed. For example, the STS-116 rescue mission was branded STS-317, because the normal mission scheduled after STS-116 was STS-117. Should the rescue mission have been needed, the crew and vehicle for STS-117 would assume the rescue mission profile and become STS-317. All potential rescue missions were to be launched with a crew of four, and would return with ten or eleven crew members, depending on the number of crew launched on the rescued shuttle. Missions were expected to last approximately eleven days. None of the planned contingency missions were ever flown.[303]

No contingency mission was planned for STS-135, the final shuttle mission. Instead, NASA planned to effect any required rescues one-by-one, using Russian Soyuz spacecraft.[304]

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
For Soviet Space Shuttle missions, see List of Buran missions.
Launch of Space Shuttle Columbia on 12 April 1981 at Pad 39A for mission STS-1

The Space Shuttle was a partially reusable low Earth orbital spacecraft system operated by NASA (the National Aeronautics and Space Administration). Its official program name was Space Transportation System (STS), taken from a 1969 plan for a system of reusable spacecraft of which it was the only item funded for development.[1] Operational missions launched numerous satellites, conducted science experiments in orbit, and participated in construction and servicing of the International Space Station (ISS). The first of four orbital test flights occurred in 1981, leading to operational flights beginning in 1982.

From 1981 to 2011 a total of 135 missions were flown, all launched from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. During that time period the fleet logged 1,322 days, 19 hours, 21 minutes and 23 seconds of flight time.[2] The longest orbital flight of the Shuttle was STS-80 at 17 days 15 hours, while the shortest flight was STS-51-L at one minute 13 seconds when the Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart during launch. The cold morning shrank an O-ring on the right solid rocket booster causing the external fuel tank to explode. The shuttles docked with Russian space station Mir nine times and visited the ISS thirty-seven times. The highest altitude (apogee) achieved by the shuttle was 386 mi (621 km) when deploying the Hubble Space Telescope.[3] The program flew a total of 355 people representing 16 countries, and with 852 total shuttle fliers.[4] The Kennedy Space Center served as the landing site for 78 missions, while 54 missions landed at Edwards Air Force Base in California and one mission landed at White Sands, New Mexico.[5]

The first orbiter built, Enterprise, was used for atmospheric flight tests (ALT) but future plans to upgrade it to orbital capability were ultimately canceled. Four fully operational orbiters were initially built: Columbia, Challenger, Discovery, and Atlantis. Challenger and Columbia were destroyed in mission accidents in 1986 and 2003 respectively, killing a total of fourteen astronauts. A fifth operational orbiter, Endeavour, was built in 1991 to replace Challenger. The Space Shuttle was retired from service upon the conclusion of STS-135 by Atlantis on 21 July 2011.[6]

Flight numberingedit
Profiles of all five orbiters at launch.

The U.S. Space Shuttle program was officially referred to as the Space Transportation System (STS). Specific shuttle missions were therefore designated with the prefix "STS".[2] Initially, the launches were given sequential numbers indicating order of launch, such as STS-7. Subsequent to the Apollo 13 mishap, due to Administrator of NASA James M. Beggs's triskaidekaphobia and consequent unwillingness to number a forthcoming flight as STS-13,[7][8][9][10] beginning in 1984, each mission was assigned a code, such as STS-41-B, with the first digit (or pair of digits for years 1990 and beyond) indicating the federal fiscal year offset into the program (so 41-B was scheduled for FY 1984, 51-A through 51-L originally for FY 1985, and the third flight in FY 1985 would have been named 51-C), the second digit indicating the launch site (1 was Kennedy Space Center and 2 was Space Launch Complex 6 at Vandenberg Air Force Base, although Vandenberg was never used), and the letter indicating scheduling sequence.[11] These codes were assigned when the launches were initially scheduled and were not changed as missions were delayed or rescheduled.[6] The codes were adopted from STS-41-B through STS-51-L (although the highest code used was actually STS-61-C), and the sequential numbers were used internally at NASA on all processing paperwork.

After the Challenger disaster, NASA returned to using a sequential numbering system, with the number counting from the beginning of the STS program. Unlike the initial system, however, the numbers were assigned based on the initial mission schedule, and did not always reflect actual launch order. This numbering scheme started at 26, with the first flight as STS-26R—the R suffix stood for "reflight" to disambiguate from prior missions. The suffix was used for two years through STS-33R, then the R was dropped.[6] As a result of the changes in systems, flights under different numbering systems could have the same number with one having a letter appended, e.g. flight STS-51 (a mission carried out by Discovery in 1993) was many years after STS-51-A (Discovery's second flight in 1984).[6] It wasn't until STS-127 in 2009 where the flight numbering system returned to a standard and consistent order.
